Dubai Islamic Bank PJSC said it’s buying Emirates Islamic Bank PJSC in an all-stock deal that will create one of the world’s largest listed Islamic-banking groups, with combined assets of about $159 billion.
As part of the transaction, DIB will issue 3.49 billion new shares to Emirates NBD Bank PJSC, the owner of Emirates Islamic, it said in an exchange filing Wednesday. The deal values the target at about 31.1 billion dirhams ($8.5 billion) based on DIB’s last close, according to Bloomberg calculations.

Two companies controlled by Indian billionaire Gautam Adani are looking to sell public bonds to raise at least 20 billion rupees ($220 million), according to people familiar with the matter, which would boost the nation’s subdued domestic public debt market.
The firms — the flagship Adani Enterprises Ltd. and Adani Power Ltd. — are working with local bond arrangers, with one offering targeted by the end of December and the other in March, the people said, asking not to be identified because the information is private. Each company is expected to raise between 10 billion rupees and 20 billion rupees, the people said. The terms are not yet final and could change.

Japan’s concerted push to bolster the yen is running into a major headwind, after the nation’s biggest life insurers slashed their currency hedging to a record low in the fiscal first half.
Nine of the largest life insurers collectively hedged 43.3% of their foreign-asset holdings with derivatives in the six months ended Sept. 30, according to Bloomberg’s analysis of their earnings reports. That’s the lowest-ever level based on data going back to 2011. The volume of currency derivatives fell 7.6%, outpacing a 1.5% decline in overseas securities.

One of Wall Street’s most reliable wagers of 2026 is starting to lose its surefire status.
The carry trade — in which investors borrow in currencies such as the yen, euro and dollar where interest rates are relatively low and put the money to work where yields are higher — has become harder to navigate after taking off last year and delivering much of this year.

Copper jumped more than 3% from an 11-month low, tracking gains in tech stocks even as doubts lingered over the durability of the AI boom and related industrial metals demand.
Three-month copper futures on the London Metal Exchange surged, trimming this month’s steep losses, which were driven by worries about the artificial intelligence trade and looming US interest-rate hikes. All six base metals on the LME saw prices rebound sharply on Thursday, a public holiday in the US.

This article is for subscribers only.
Good morning...
I’m Pratigya Vajpayee in Mumbai, where the rupee is riding the rally in stocks.
Stock and currency bulls in India remain firmly in charge as the Nifty’s world-beating equity run rolls on. Jensen Huang’s return at Nvidia has done little to lift the mood for the global AI trade and that is working to India’s advantage. The Nifty jumped nearly 2% on Wednesday while the rupee climbed to an eight-month high. Much of the momentum can be attributed to a surge in foreign equity inflows. Global funds have bought a record $14.7 billion worth of Indian shares on a net basis so far in November. Today’s Markets Buzz section explains why the rupee’s rally may have room to run.
One note of caution: US tariff rates announced Wednesday have put pressure on India to agree to a trade deal or face a higher levy, leaving exporters and investors with little clarity on the trade outlook. The US plans to impose a 17% tariff on Indian goods. The rate would be hiked to 25% if India fails to secure a trade deal.
Asian stocks are up in early trading on Thursday after dip buyers helped drive a late recovery on Wall Street, bringing some stability to markets after doubts over the AI trade spurred a flight to Treasuries. A hawkish member of the Bank of Japan’s policy board called for early action to keep raising the BOJ’s benchmark rate, supporting market expectations for a rate hike next month.
“I believe that the Bank needs to bring the policy rate to the neutral level soon,” Naoki Tamura said Thursday in a speech to local business leaders in Yamanashi, west of Tokyo. A neutral level refers to a level neither restrictive or stimulative for the economy.
